text:
Áine, also written Enya, is an Irish goddess, heroine, or spirit. Her name means brightness or splendor. Irish legend offers several figures of this name. Historical figures of the name tend to be male and connected with the Limerick and north Kerry area of Munster. Mythological figures are female and typically connected to the same area. The name is also found as far away as Ulster. The most prominent Áines of myth may ultimately be the same figure or may derive from the same original.

Áine of Knockainy is usually described as a fairy queen. She is probably a diminished goddess. She inhabits a hill near storied Lough Gur in east County Limerick. Several scholars connect her with Anu, also called Danu, the great goddess of Munster. Anu gave her name to the Tuatha Dé Danann, the tribe of the goddess Danu.

Indications point to a sun goddess. She was connected with solar wells like Tobar Áine near Lissan in Ulster. She was linked with the sun goddess Grian, her sister. At other times she is described as related to Finnen, white, an obscure goddess of the Lough Gur region. As a sun goddess, Áine could assume the form of an unbeatable horse, Lair Derg, the red mare.

Áine's feast was held on either Midsummer night, the summer solstice on June 21, or on Lughnasa, the Celtic feast on August 1. At that time straw torches were waved over animals. The animals were then driven up the slopes of Knockainy to solicit her protection. She is sometimes called Áine Chlair, either from the cliars or torches used in such ceremonies, or from Cliu or Cliach, the ancient name for the territory. Locally she was called the best-hearted woman that ever lived. She was reported seen on the slopes of her mountain even into recent times, offering help to those in need.

Áine's lovers included gods and mortals. Among the gods was the sea god Manannán mac Lir. Her brother Aillén fell in love with Manannán's wife. Manannán in turn loved Áine. He gave his wife to Aillén in exchange for the charms of Áine. A variant has Áine as daughter rather than lover to Manannán. Although a lustful goddess, she also has a matronly aspect. Her birth chair can be seen on the mountain Knockadoon.

Áine was the lover of Maurice, also called Muiris, the human Earl of Desmond. He stole her cloak in order to capture her, the swan maiden motif. Once captured, she bore him a son, Geróid Iarla, or Gerald the waterbird. Maurice was warned against showing any surprise at their magical son's behavior. He stayed composed until Geróid was fully grown and showed he could shrink almost into invisibility. When his father called out in astonishment, Geróid disappeared. He is said to live still in Lough Gur and to ride around it every seven years on a white horse.

The descendants of Áine's son, the Geraldines or Fitzgeralds, long claimed sovereignty in western Munster through this descent from the goddess of the land. In the literary tradition she was regarded as a territorial goddess of north Munster and the ancestress of the Fitzgeralds.

Áine did not always go willingly to her lovers. She was responsible for the death of the hero Étar. He died of a broken heart when she rejected him. She also resisted Ailill Olom, who took her against her will. She ripped off his ear in her unsuccessful fight. The child of the rape was Eógan. Some scholars call this story an invention of his descendants, the Eóganacht rulers, to affirm control of the lands under Áine's sovereignty.

Some legends connect Áine with madness. Those who sat on her stone chair went mad. If they sat there three times, they would never recover their wits. Those who were already mad could regain their sanity through the same process.

Áine of Donegal came from the parish of Teelin in the townland of Cruachlann, near another mountain called Cnoc Áine. There she was said to have been a human woman who disappeared into the mountain to escape a savage father. She now spends her time spinning sunbeams, suggesting that the folkloric figure disguises an ancient sun goddess. A folk verse from the area has her telling discontented wives how to weaken their husbands with corn warm from the kiln and sheep's milk on the boil.

Áine of the Fenian Cycle was the daughter of either the fairy king Cuilenn or a Scottish king. She was the lover of Fionn mac Cumhaill, by whom she had two sons. Áine and her sister Milucra fought for Fionn's affections. Milucra turned him into a graybearded ancient who would be uncompelled by lust. Áine restored him to youth with a magical drink. Fionn, however, married neither of the sisters.
objective: To record the several Irish figures named Áine and their legends.
